shortQuestions: In an alcohol the –OH group is attached to a saturated (sp³) carbon of an alkyl group, e.g. CH₃CH₂OH; in a phenol it is attached directly to a carbon of a benzene ring (sp²), e.g. C₆H₅OH.

As a result phenol is weakly acidic (its anion is resonance-stabilised) and reacts with NaOH, gives a violet colour with FeCl₃ and readily undergoes ring substitution; alcohols are neutral and do not react with NaOH.
C₄H₉OH has four structural isomeric alcohols:
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH — n-butyl alcohol, butan-1-ol (1°).
CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ — sec-butyl alcohol, butan-2-ol (2°; it also has two enantiomers).
(CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH — isobutyl alcohol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol (1°).
(CH₃)₃COH — tert-butyl alcohol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol (3°).

Lucas reagent is anhydrous ZnCl₂ in concentrated HCl. The alcohol is shaken with the reagent at room temperature; it is converted into an alkyl chloride, which is insoluble and makes the solution cloudy.

Tertiary alcohols give cloudiness immediately; secondary alcohols within about 5 minutes; primary alcohols show no cloudiness at room temperature (only on heating). The rate follows carbocation stability, 3° > 2° > 1°.
When phenol loses H⁺, the negative charge on the phenoxide ion is delocalised over the benzene ring by resonance (into the ortho and para positions), which stabilises it.
In an alkoxide ion RO⁻ the charge stays on oxygen, and the alkyl group (+I) even intensifies it. So phenol (pKa ≈ 10) ionises much more than alcohols (pKa ≈ 16–18).
Alcohols are classified by the number of carbon atoms bonded to the carbon that carries –OH.
Primary (1°): one carbon (or none), RCH₂OH, e.g. ethanol. Secondary (2°): two carbons, R₂CHOH, e.g. propan-2-ol. Tertiary (3°): three carbons, R₃COH, e.g. 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
In alcohols and ethers the lone pairs on oxygen are localised and freely available, so the oxygen readily accepts a proton to form an oxonium ion (ROH₂⁺, R₂OH⁺).
In phenol the oxygen lone pairs are partly delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, so they are less available for bonding with H⁺. Phenol is therefore much harder to protonate.

Heating a mixture of two different alcohols R–OH and R′–OH with concentrated H₂SO₄ gives a mixture of three ethers (R–O–R, R′–O–R′ and R–O–R′), which are difficult to separate; secondary and tertiary alcohols also dehydrate to alkenes.
So asymmetric (mixed) ethers are made by Williamson's synthesis instead: R–ONa + R′–X → R–O–R′ + NaX.
Alkene: bromine adds across the C=C bond; the brown colour disappears but no precipitate forms (a colourless dibromide), e.g. CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂Br–CH₂Br.

Phenol: bromine substitutes on the highly activated ring at room temperature without a catalyst; the colour disappears and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms, with HBr: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH↓ + 3HBr.
The diazonium group –N₂⁺ can leave as nitrogen gas, N₂, an extremely stable molecule (strong triple bond) — an excellent leaving group, and its escape is favoured by the increase in entropy.

Benzenediazonium salts are stabilised only slightly by resonance with the ring, so they are stable only at 0–5 °C. On warming they lose N₂ and the aryl cation is attacked by water, giving phenol: C₆H₅N₂⁺ + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + N₂ + H⁺.
Oxidation of an alcohol removes the hydrogen of –OH and a hydrogen from the carbon bearing –OH (the carbinol carbon) to form C=O.

In a tertiary alcohol R₃C–OH the carbinol carbon has no hydrogen, so it cannot be oxidised without breaking a C–C bond; it resists mild oxidising agents (only drastic oxidation degrades the molecule).
longQuestions: (a) Dehydration of alcohol: ethanol in excess is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 140 °C: 2C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅–O–C₂H₅ + H₂O. Mechanism: the alcohol is protonated (C₂H₅OH₂⁺); a second ethanol molecule attacks it (SN2), losing water; then loss of H⁺ gives the ether. (At 170 °C ethene is formed instead.)
Williamson's synthesis: sodium ethoxide reacts with ethyl bromide (SN2): C₂H₅ONa + C₂H₅Br → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + NaBr. It is suitable for symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers (the halide should be primary).

(b) Reactions: (i) with hot concentrated HI: C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + HI → C₂H₅OH + C₂H₅I; with excess HI, 2C₂H₅I + H₂O. (ii) With cold concentrated H₂SO₄ it forms a soluble oxonium salt (C₂H₅)₂OH⁺HSO₄⁻; with PCl₅ on heating: C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + PCl₅ → 2C₂H₅Cl + POCl₃. (Ether slowly forms explosive peroxides in air.)

(c) Physical properties: colourless, volatile liquid with a sweet smell; boiling point 34.6 °C (lower than isomeric alcohols, since ethers cannot form hydrogen bonds among themselves); slightly soluble in water (H-bonds with water) but miscible with organic solvents; good solvent for fats and oils; less dense than water; highly flammable; once used as an anaesthetic.

(a) Phenols are compounds in which an –OH group is attached directly to a carbon of an aromatic ring, e.g. phenol C₆H₅OH, cresols. Preparation: (i) From benzenesulphonic acid: fuse sodium benzenesulphonate with NaOH: C₆H₅SO₃Na + 2NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + Na₂SO₃ + H₂O, then acidify: C₆H₅ONa + HCl → C₆H₅OH + NaCl. (ii) Dow process: C₆H₅Cl + 2NaOH —350 °C, 200 atm→ C₆H₅ONa + NaCl + H₂O, then acidify. (iii) From benzenediazonium chloride by warming with water: C₆H₅N₂Cl + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + N₂ + HCl. (iv) From cumene: cumene is oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide, which with dilute acid gives phenol and acetone.

(b) Acidic behaviour: phenol is a weak acid (pKa ≈ 10): C₆H₅OH + H₂O ⇌ C₆H₅O⁻ + H₃O⁺. It reacts with Na (H₂ evolved) and with NaOH: C₆H₅OH + NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + H₂O, but it is weaker than carbonic acid and does not liberate CO₂ from NaHCO₃.

Reason: the phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance, the negative charge spreading over the ortho and para carbons. Electron-withdrawing groups (–NO₂) increase acidity (2,4,6-trinitrophenol, picric acid, is quite strong); electron-donating groups (–CH₃) decrease it.

Structure: in phenol the –OH is bonded to an sp² carbon of the benzene ring. A lone pair on oxygen overlaps with the ring π system (resonance), giving the C–O bond partial double-bond character (136 pm, shorter than in alcohols) and increasing electron density at the ortho and para positions. The molecule is planar and the O–H is polar, so phenol forms hydrogen bonds (m.p. 41 °C, b.p. 182 °C, moderately soluble in water).

Reactions of the –OH group: acidic — with Na and NaOH forms sodium phenoxide; esterification — C₆H₅OH + CH₃COCl → C₆H₅OCOCH₃ + HCl; ether formation — C₆H₅ONa + CH₃I → C₆H₅OCH₃ + NaI; FeCl₃ test — violet colour; reduction with zinc dust gives benzene: C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO.

Ring (electrophilic substitution) reactions — highly activated, ortho/para: bromination with bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol; dilute HNO₃ gives o- and p-nitrophenol, concentrated HNO₃ gives picric acid; sulphonation gives o-/p-hydroxybenzenesulphonic acid.
Other reactions: Kolbe's reaction — sodium phenoxide + CO₂ (125 °C, pressure), then acid, gives salicylic acid; condensation with formaldehyde gives bakelite; hydrogenation (Ni) gives cyclohexanol.

(a) Structure: alcohols contain –OH bonded to an sp³ carbon; oxygen is sp³-hybridised with two lone pairs and a C–O–H angle of about 105°. The O–H bond is polar, so alcohols form hydrogen bonds (higher boiling points; lower alcohols miscible with water).

Synthesis: (i) hydration of alkenes: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O —H₂SO₄→ CH₃CH₂OH; (ii) hydrolysis of alkyl halides: RX + KOH(aq) → ROH + KX; (iii) reduction of aldehydes and ketones with LiAlH₄, NaBH₄ or H₂/Ni (aldehyde → 1°, ketone → 2°); (iv) Grignard reagents with carbonyl compounds; (v) fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ —yeast→ 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.

Reactions: with Na → alkoxide + H₂; with HX, PCl₅, PCl₃ or SOCl₂ → alkyl halides; dehydration with concentrated H₂SO₄ (170 °C → alkene, 140 °C → ether); oxidation — 1° → aldehyde → carboxylic acid, 2° → ketone, 3° resistant; esterification: RCOOH + R′OH ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O (H₂SO₄ catalyst).

(b) Alcohols are very weakly acidic because the O–H bond is polar: they react with active metals releasing hydrogen, 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂. They are weaker acids than water (the alkyl group's +I effect destabilises the alkoxide ion), so they do not turn blue litmus red or react with NaOH.

(a) From Grignard reagents and carbonyl compounds, followed by hydrolysis: formaldehyde gives primary alcohols — HCHO + CH₃MgI → CH₃CH₂OMgI → CH₃CH₂OH; other aldehydes give secondary alcohols — CH₃CHO + CH₃MgI → (CH₃)₂CHOH; ketones give tertiary alcohols — (CH₃)₂CO + CH₃MgI → (CH₃)₃COH. (Esters give tertiary alcohols with two moles of RMgX.)

(b)(i) Ethene: C₂H₅OH —conc. H₂SO₄, 170 °C→ CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O. (ii) Ethyl acetate: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ (conc. H₂SO₄) CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. (iii) Acetone: oxidation of propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂CHOH + [O] —K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄→ (CH₃)₂CO + H₂O (or Cu at 300 °C). (iv) Formaldehyde: oxidation of methanol, CH₃OH + [O] → HCHO + H₂O (Cu or Ag catalyst at 300 °C, or PCC).
(c, d) Structural formulas: i. pentan-2-ol: CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₂CH₂CH₃. ii. 3,4-dimethylhexan-2-ol: CH₃–CH(OH)–CH(CH₃)–CH(CH₃)–CH₂CH₃. iii. 4-methylpent-3-en-2-ol: CH₃–CH(OH)–CH=C(CH₃)₂.

iv. 3,4-dimethyl-2-nitrophenol: a benzene ring with –OH at C1, –NO₂ at C2 and –CH₃ at C3 and C4. v. 2,3-dimethoxy-4-methylpentane: CH₃–CH(OCH₃)–CH(OCH₃)–CH(CH₃)–CH₃. (Part (c) prints no structures to be named, so only part (d) can be answered.)
